summary.text: A standard candle is an astronomical object that has a known luminosity.
By comparing that known luminosity with an object's observed brightness, astronomers compute its distance using the inverse-square law.
Several methods on the cosmic distance ladder rely on them, and each rung of the ladder gives information used to find the next.

items.prompt: Two street lamps are known to use the same bulb, but one looks much fainter. What does that tell you?

options.label: The fainter lamp is farther away
The fainter lamp is a weaker bulb
The fainter lamp is on a taller pole
The fainter lamp is switched on for fewer hours

items.explain: Comparing known luminosity with observed brightness gives distance by the inverse-square law.

items.prompt: Astronomers find a new class of exploding star and want to use it as a yardstick. What must they pin down first?

options.label: Its colour, measured from a single bright member
Its age, taken from the oldest member they see
Its true brightness, found from members at well-known distances
Its speed, estimated from members in the same cluster

items.explain: Calibration means determining the candle's exact absolute magnitude, which needs enough members of the class with well-known distances.

items.prompt: Why is it risky to use a standard candle's brightness on a very distant object?

options.label: The candle's brightness changes whenever it is observed
It may not truly belong to the class, giving a wrong distance
Distant objects are always brighter than nearby ones
The inverse-square law stops working beyond a set range

items.explain: Recognising members of the class is a problem, and at extreme distances it can be quite serious.

items.prompt: In the 1950s astronomers learned that the nearby stars used for calibration were a different type from those in nearby galaxies. What happened to distance estimates?

options.label: They roughly halved for nearby galaxies and the Milky Way
They stayed the same but became more precise
They could no longer be made for nearby galaxies
They roughly doubled for nearby galaxies and the Milky Way's size

items.explain: The distant population II stars were much brighter than believed, which doubled estimates of distance to globular clusters, nearby galaxies and the Milky Way's diameter.

items.prompt: Why do astronomers use a ladder of methods rather than one technique?

options.label: No single technique can measure distances at every range
Each method gives the same answer, so they check one another
Each method works only on one kind of star
One method would take longer than a human lifetime

items.explain: Because no single technique works at all ranges, each rung gives information used to determine the next higher rung.

items.prompt: By watching a gravitational wave's waveform, astronomers can work out the power of its source. What does that make the source?

options.label: A standard siren of known loudness
A source whose colour reveals its age
A source of unknown brightness that can never be used for distance
A fixed rung at the base of the ladder with no assumptions

items.explain: Observing the waveform gives the chirp mass and thence the power, so such a source is a standard siren of known loudness.

paragraphs.heading: A light of known strength
paragraphs.text: A standard candle is an object in space whose true brightness, called its luminosity, is known. Astronomers compare that known luminosity with how bright the object looks from here, and the inverse-square law then gives its distance. The term was coined by Henrietta Swan Leavitt.

paragraphs.heading: Why astronomers need them
paragraphs.text: Distances can be measured directly only for objects that are fairly close, within about a thousand parsecs of Earth. Farther out, astronomers rely on a chain of methods called the cosmic distance ladder, because no single technique works at every range. One method covers nearby objects, another reaches a little farther, and each step supplies what is needed to set up the next. Several of these methods depend on standard candles.

paragraphs.heading: Turning brightness into distance
paragraphs.text: An object's brightness can be expressed as its absolute magnitude, worked out from the logarithm of how luminous it would appear from 10 parsecs away. Its apparent magnitude is how bright it looks to the observer, and the two together give the distance d in parsecs: d = 10^((m−M+5)/5). The difference between the two magnitudes is called the distance modulus. Objects can also look dimmer and redder because of interstellar extinction, so this must be corrected for, above all when the object sits in a dusty or gassy region.

paragraphs.heading: Two built-in problems
paragraphs.text: Every kind of standard candle faces two problems. The main one is calibration: pinning down exactly how bright members of the class truly are. That means defining the class clearly and finding enough members whose distances are already well known. The second is making sure an object really belongs to the class, and at extreme distances, which is just where such a yardstick would help most, this can be a serious problem.

paragraphs.heading: How standard are they
paragraphs.text: Astronomers keep asking how standard these candles really are. Type Ia supernovae at known distances all seem to share the same brightness once adjusted for the shape of their light curve, yet distant ones might behave differently from nearby ones. That matters, because these supernovae are crucial for picking the right model of the cosmos. If their behavior does change with distance and this is ignored, estimates such as the density of matter could be badly skewed.

paragraphs.heading: A lesson from Cepheids
paragraphs.text: The history of Cepheid variable stars shows this worry is not just theory. In the 1950s, Walter Baade found that the nearby Cepheids used for calibration were a different type from those used to measure distances to nearby galaxies. The nearby ones were population I stars, much richer in metals, while the distant population II stars were really much brighter than assumed. Correcting this doubled the estimated distances to globular clusters and nearby galaxies, and the estimated width of the Milky Way.

paragraphs.heading: New candles and sirens
paragraphs.text: Kilonovae have recently been suggested as another type of standard candle. Gravitational waves offer a related tool. As two neutron stars or black holes spiral in toward each other, their orbit shrinks and the frequency of their waves rises. From the shape of the signal, scientists can compute a number called the chirp mass and from it the power the waves carry, making the pair a standard siren of known loudness.
